# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of significant epicardial coronary artery stenosis [1,2]. First described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the phenomenon has been increasingly recognized as a distinct clinical disorder rather than a benign angiographic curiosity [1,3]. Patients with CSFP frequently present with recurrent chest pain, and the condition contributes to substantial healthcare utilization and impaired quality of life [4,5].

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP is most reliably quantified using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count method, originally developed by Gibson et al., which provides an objective, reproducible measure of coronary flow [6,7]. A corrected TIMI frame count exceeding two standard deviations above the normal mean for a given vessel is generally used to define slow flow [6,8]. The condition must be distinguished from the no-reflow phenomenon, which typically occurs after percutaneous coronary intervention or acute myocardial infarction [9]. CSFP is reported in approximately 1–7% of patients undergoing diagnostic coronary angiography for suspected ischemia [2,4].

## Pathophysiology

The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying CSFP remain incompletely understood, but several interrelated processes have been proposed [3,10]. Microvascular dysfunction is widely regarded as central, with abnormalities in the small resistance vessels leading to increased microvascular resistance [10,11]. Endothelial dysfunction, evidenced by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilation, has been consistently demonstrated in affected patients [11,12]. Histopathological studies of endomyocardial biopsies have revealed fibromuscular hyperplasia, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial degeneration in the small coronary arteries [13].

Diffuse atherosclerosis, even in angiographically "normal" vessels, may also contribute; intravascular ultrasound studies have detected subclinical atheromatous changes and intimal thickening in patients with CSFP [14]. Inflammation appears to play a role, with elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and other inflammatory markers reported [15,16]. Oxidative stress and an imbalance between vasoconstrictor and vasodilator mediators, including elevated endothelin-1, have also been implicated [12,17]. Additionally, increased platelet activation and abnormal hemorheological properties, such as elevated blood viscosity, have been described [18,19].

## Clinical Associations and Risk Factors

CSFP demonstrates a male predominance and is frequently associated with cardiovascular risk factors such as smoking, metabolic syndrome, obesity, and insulin resistance [4,20]. Several studies have linked CSFP to elevated body mass index and dyslipidemia [20,21]. The condition has been associated with electrocardiographic abnormalities, including prolonged QT dispersion and fragmented QRS complexes, which may underlie the increased propensity for ventricular arrhythmias observed in some patients [22,23]. Importantly, CSFP is not entirely benign; cases of acute coronary syndromes, life-threatening arrhythmias, and even sudden cardiac death have been reported [24,25].

## Clinical Presentation and Prognosis

The most common presentation is recurrent angina, which may occur both at rest and with exertion, and a significant proportion of patients require repeated hospital admissions [4,5]. While the long-term prognosis is generally considered favorable in terms of mortality, the persistent symptom burden and recurrent chest pain markedly reduce quality of life [5,25]. Long-term follow-up studies suggest that major adverse cardiovascular events, although uncommon, do occur in a subset of patients [25].

## Management

There is no universally established treatment for CSFP, and management remains largely empirical [3,26]. Dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, particularly diltiazem, have shown efficacy in improving TIMI frame counts and reducing anginal symptoms [26,27]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilatory properties, has demonstrated benefit in improving coronary flow and endothelial function [28]. Statins may exert favorable effects through their pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilizing actions [29]. Other agents, including dipyridamole, trimetazapine, and mibefradil, have been investigated with variable results [27,30]. Lifestyle modification, smoking cessation, and aggressive risk-factor control remain important adjuncts [20,29].

## Conclusion

CSFP is an underrecognized but clinically important angiographic and pathophysiological entity that bridges epicardial coronary disease and microvascular dysfunction [2,10]. Despite advances in understanding its mechanisms—encompassing endothelial dysfunction, microvascular abnormality, inflammation, and subclinical atherosclerosis—much remains to be elucidated [10,13,15]. Standardized diagnostic criteria based on the TIMI frame count have improved consistency in research and clinical practice [6,8]. Future studies should focus on randomized controlled trials to establish evidence-based therapeutic strategies and on long-term prospective cohorts to better define prognosis [26,30].
